Why Do I Keep Getting a Sore Mouth From My Dentures?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Denture soreness is one of the most common concerns amongst denture wearers, and if you have found yourself searching for answers after waking up with a painful or irritated mouth, you are certainly not alone. Many adults in the UK experience recurring discomfort from their dentures, yet often assume it is something they simply have to tolerate. In reality, a persistently sore mouth from dentures can signal that something needs attention — whether that is an adjustment to the fit, a change in oral health, or a closer look at the condition of the denture itself.

Understanding why denture-related soreness occurs can help you make informed decisions about your dental health. This article explains the most common causes of denture-related oral discomfort, what may be happening clinically beneath the surface, practical advice to help reduce irritation, and guidance on when it may be appropriate to seek professional dental support.

Why Does My Mouth Keep Getting Sore From Dentures?

A sore mouth from dentures is most commonly caused by ill-fitting dentures, changes in the shape of the jawbone over time, fungal infections such as denture stomatitis, or inadequate denture hygiene. Persistent soreness warrants professional dental assessment to identify the underlying cause and explore appropriate solutions.

Common Causes of Denture-Related Mouth Soreness

Denture-related soreness can have several underlying causes, and in many cases, more than one factor may be contributing at the same time. Understanding these causes can help you have a more informed conversation with your dental professional.

Ill-fitting dentures are perhaps the most frequently cited reason for ongoing discomfort. Dentures that do not sit correctly against the gums create friction and pressure points, leading to localised soreness, ulceration, or general irritation. This poor fit is not always present from the outset — dentures that once fitted well can become loose or ill-fitting over time as the underlying bone and gum tissue naturally changes in shape.

Bone resorption is a significant contributing factor that many denture wearers are unaware of. After teeth are lost, the jawbone gradually diminishes in volume because it no longer receives the stimulation it once did from natural tooth roots. This process means the ridge upon which the denture rests becomes narrower and flatter over the years, creating a mismatch between the denture base and the supporting tissue.

Newly fitted dentures can also cause temporary soreness during the adjustment period, as the mouth adapts to the new appliance. This is generally expected and tends to settle, though persistent discomfort beyond the initial weeks should always be reviewed.

Sharp edges or damaged dentures may cause localised cuts or ulcers if a crack or worn area creates an abrasive surface against the soft tissue.

Denture Stomatitis: A Clinical Explanation

One of the more frequently overlooked causes of a sore mouth in denture wearers is a condition known as denture stomatitis. This is a form of oral candidiasis — a fungal infection caused by an overgrowth of Candida albicans, a yeast organism that is naturally present in the mouth in small quantities.

Under certain conditions — particularly when a denture is worn continuously overnight, or when denture hygiene is not thorough — the warm, moist environment beneath the denture base creates ideal conditions for this organism to multiply. The result is inflammation of the palatal mucosa (the tissue of the roof of the mouth), which can appear red, swollen, or dotted with small raised areas. It is worth noting that denture stomatitis does not always cause pain — some patients have no obvious symptoms — but it can contribute to a generalised soreness, a burning sensation, or persistent discomfort.

This condition is more prevalent than many patients realise. Studies suggest it affects a significant proportion of complete denture wearers. Treatment typically involves antifungal medication prescribed by a dental or medical professional, alongside guidance on improving denture hygiene practices. If you want a deeper clinical overview, see our related guide on whether dental implants may help with denture stomatitis.

Maintaining a thorough denture-cleaning routine and removing dentures at night are two of the most effective steps a patient can take to reduce the risk of this type of infection.

How Changes in Your Mouth Affect Denture Fit Over Time

It is a common misconception that once a denture has been made and fits well, it will continue to do so indefinitely. In practice, the oral environment is dynamic and changes continuously over time, which means a denture that fitted well when first made may gradually become less well-adapted to the mouth.

Gum and bone changes occur naturally following tooth loss and continue throughout life. As the alveolar bone (the ridge of bone that supported your natural teeth) resorbs, the gum tissue above it also changes shape. A denture made to fit the original anatomy will slowly begin to rock, tilt, or create uneven pressure as this process progresses.

Weight changes in the patient can also affect facial and oral soft tissue, which in turn influences how a denture sits and functions.

Ageing of the denture material itself is another factor. Acrylic denture bases may gradually distort, become porous, or suffer minor damage over years of use. Porous surfaces can harbour bacteria and fungi, contributing both to oral health issues and to changes in the structural fit of the appliance.

Dental professionals generally recommend that dentures are reviewed regularly — even when a patient feels no obvious discomfort — to monitor fit and oral tissue health. Over time, dentures may require relining, rebasing, or replacement to maintain function and comfort.

Signs and Symptoms That May Indicate a Problem

Recognising the signs of denture-related problems can help you seek advice promptly, before minor issues become more persistent.

Common symptoms that may indicate something needs attention include:

  • Persistent or recurring soreness in specific areas of the gum ridge or palate
  • Redness or inflammation beneath the denture, particularly on the roof of the mouth
  • Ulcers or sore spots that develop shortly after inserting the denture
  • A burning sensation in the mouth, particularly under the upper denture
  • Difficulty chewing or speaking due to denture movement or instability
  • Clicking, rocking, or slipping of the denture during normal use
  • Denture adhesive dependency as a substitute for proper fit — while adhesives can be a helpful short-term aid, relying on them consistently may indicate the denture requires professional assessment

It is also worth noting that some patients experience angular cheilitis — soreness and cracking at the corners of the mouth — which can be associated with denture-related fungal infections or with changes in bite height caused by worn or ill-fitting dentures.

None of these symptoms should be considered normal or something to simply endure. Each can usually be addressed with appropriate professional guidance.

When to Seek Professional Dental Assessment

There are certain circumstances in which arranging a professional dental review would be particularly appropriate, even if symptoms appear mild or have been present for some time.

You may wish to seek dental advice if:

  • Soreness has persisted for more than two weeks despite removing the denture and allowing tissue to rest
  • Ulcers are present that do not resolve after the denture is left out
  • Swelling or bleeding occurs in the gum tissue beneath the denture
  • There is a noticeable change in fit — such as increased looseness or rocking — compared to when the denture was first made
  • You experience pain when chewing or have begun avoiding certain foods as a result
  • There is visible redness or a velvety red area on the palate beneath an upper denture, which may suggest denture stomatitis

It is also important to be aware that any oral mucosal changes — including persistent ulcers, white patches, or red areas — that do not resolve within two to three weeks should be evaluated by a dental professional, as part of routine oral health monitoring.

For patients who have experienced significant bone loss beneath their dentures or who find that repeated denture adjustments are not providing adequate comfort, it may be worth discussing whether there are longer-term tooth replacement options to consider. You can find information about dental implants as an alternative to dentures on our main treatment pages.

The Role of Denture Hygiene in Preventing Soreness

Good denture hygiene is one of the most accessible and effective ways to reduce the risk of recurring oral soreness. Many patients are surprised to learn that dentures require as much careful maintenance as natural teeth — if not more so, given the different materials involved.

Key denture hygiene practices include:

  • Remove and rinse dentures after every meal to prevent food particles from collecting beneath the base
  • Brush the denture thoroughly each day using a soft-bristled brush and non-abrasive denture cleaner — ordinary toothpaste is generally too abrasive for acrylic and can create microscopic scratches that harbour bacteria
  • Soak dentures overnight in a denture-cleaning solution or cold water — this both cleans the appliance and allows the gum tissue to rest, reducing the risk of denture stomatitis
  • Clean your mouth — gums, tongue, and palate — each morning before inserting your denture, using a soft toothbrush or damp cloth
  • Never use boiling water to clean or soak dentures, as this can warp the material and affect the fit
  • Handle dentures carefully over a folded towel or basin of water to reduce the risk of accidental breakage

Patients who sleep in their dentures are at significantly higher risk of fungal infections and gum tissue deterioration. The NHS and most dental professionals advise removing dentures at night to allow mucosal tissue to recover.

Prevention and Ongoing Oral Health Advice

Beyond denture hygiene, there are broader oral health habits that can help denture wearers maintain comfort and reduce the likelihood of recurring soreness.

Regular dental check-ups remain important even after all natural teeth have been lost. During a denture review appointment, a dental professional can assess the fit of the appliance, examine the oral tissues for any signs of change, and recommend adjustments where needed. Routine appointments also provide the opportunity for an oral cancer screening examination, which is a valuable preventative health measure regardless of denture status.

A well-balanced diet supports healthy gum tissue and general oral health. Staying well hydrated is also beneficial, as dry mouth — caused by certain medications or health conditions — can increase friction between the denture and the mucosa, contributing to soreness.

Avoid using denture adhesives as a long-term substitute for a well-fitting denture. If you find you are increasing the amount of adhesive used just to keep the denture in place, this suggests the fit may have changed and a professional review would be worthwhile.

For patients who are finding that conventional dentures are becoming increasingly difficult to manage or are causing persistent discomfort, it may also be worth exploring implant-retained options. Implant-supported dentures offer greater stability by anchoring the prosthesis to implants placed within the jawbone, which can reduce movement and pressure on the soft tissue.

Key Points to Remember

  • A sore mouth from dentures is not something you simply have to tolerate — in most cases, the underlying cause can be identified and addressed.
  • Ill-fitting dentures are a common cause of soreness and often result from natural changes in the jawbone and gum tissue over time.
  • Denture stomatitis (a fungal infection beneath the denture) is more common than many patients realise and can be effectively managed with appropriate treatment and hygiene improvements.
  • Removing dentures overnight and maintaining a thorough daily cleaning routine are among the most effective preventative steps available.
  • Regular dental reviews — even without obvious symptoms — are important for monitoring denture fit and oral tissue health.
  • Persistent or unexplained oral changes that do not resolve within two to three weeks should always be assessed by a dental professional.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to get used to new dentures?

Most patients find that minor soreness and adjustment challenges settle within a few weeks of receiving new dentures, as the mouth adapts to the appliance. However, the timeline varies between individuals. If discomfort continues beyond three to four weeks, or if specific sore spots or ulcers persist, it is advisable to contact your dental practice for a review appointment. Minor adjustments to the denture base are a routine part of the fitting process and should not be seen as a sign that something has gone wrong.

Can wearing dentures overnight cause health problems?

Wearing dentures continuously without removing them overnight significantly increases the risk of developing denture stomatitis — a fungal infection of the oral mucosa beneath the denture. It also deprives the gum tissue of the opportunity to rest and recover from the pressure of the appliance throughout the day. Most dental professionals advise removing dentures at night and storing them in water or a suitable soaking solution. This simple habit can make a meaningful difference to long-term oral health and denture comfort.

Why does my mouth feel sore even after having my dentures adjusted?

If soreness persists after a professional adjustment, there may be more than one contributing factor. For example, if a fungal infection such as denture stomatitis is also present, soreness may continue until this is treated — regardless of how well the denture fits mechanically. In some cases, significant bone resorption means the tissue base upon which the denture rests has changed considerably, requiring more extensive relining or the consideration of alternative options. A thorough clinical review will help identify all contributing factors.

What is denture stomatitis and how is it treated?

Denture stomatitis is an inflammation of the oral mucosa — usually the palate — caused by an overgrowth of Candida fungi, often associated with continuous denture wearing, poor denture hygiene, or a dry mouth. It may appear as redness or a velvety red area on the roof of the mouth beneath an upper denture. Treatment typically involves antifungal medication (such as a miconazole oral gel or nystatin suspension), improved denture hygiene, and removal of the denture at night. Your dental professional can advise on the most appropriate course of action based on a clinical assessment.

How often should dentures be professionally reviewed?

Most dental professionals recommend that dentures are reviewed at least once a year, even if no obvious problems are apparent. This allows the practitioner to check the fit and condition of the appliance, examine the oral tissues, and carry out a routine oral health assessment including an oral cancer check. As bone resorption continues gradually over the years, early identification of fit changes can prevent more significant problems — such as tissue damage or accelerated bone loss — from developing.

Could my sore mouth be related to something other than the denture fit?

It is possible. While denture fit and hygiene are the most common causes of denture-related soreness, other factors can contribute. These include dry mouth caused by medications, nutritional deficiencies (such as vitamin B12 or iron deficiency), ill health, or unrelated mucosal conditions. Certain medications are also known to affect oral tissue health. If soreness does not improve after denture-related causes have been addressed, or if you notice any unusual changes in the appearance of the oral tissues, a dental professional can carry out a thorough examination to help determine the cause.

Conclusion

Recurring soreness from dentures is a common and understandably frustrating experience, but it is rarely something that simply has to be accepted. In the majority of cases, there is an identifiable cause — whether that is a change in the fit of the appliance, a fungal infection of the oral mucosa, inadequate denture hygiene, or a combination of factors — and an appropriate course of action can be recommended following professional assessment.

A sore mouth from dentures most often reflects a need for either a clinical adjustment or a change in home-care routine. Simple measures such as removing dentures overnight, maintaining a thorough daily cleaning routine, and attending regular dental reviews can all contribute meaningfully to long-term comfort and oral health.

If symptoms persist or if you have noticed changes in the appearance of your mouth that concern you, it is always worth seeking professional guidance. For patients who are exploring longer-term solutions to denture-related difficulties, speaking with a dental professional about the full range of options available — including implant-supported restorations — may also be a valuable conversation to have. You can learn more about tooth replacement options on our website.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
